routes.description: Establish that objective evaluative facts are required to account for rational assessment and that moral appearances can provide defeasible justification without first earning support through best-explanation reasoning.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supports objective moral facts against desire-based and projectivist alternatives, establishes a defensible appearance-based source of prima facie justification, and connects that epistemology to basic moral knowledge.

motionBridge.description: Connect the case for irreducible evaluative facts with a route from moral appearances to justified moral belief and knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Show that rationally assessing desires, actions, and suffering requires truth-valued evaluative standards rather than attitudes alone.
Establish that appearances confer defeasible prima facie justification and are epistemically prior to explanatory inference.
Show that understanding evaluative and experiential subject matter can justify elementary moral judgments as instances of a priori knowledge.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how evaluative judgments can shape desires, emotions, and conduct rather than merely projecting antecedent attitudes.
Identify necessary judgments that resist reduction to linguistic or conceptual analyticity and thereby support broader rationalism.

routes.description: Establish that normative reasons depend on an agent's desires and deliberative standpoint, while moral belief lacks justification because objective moral facts are unnecessary in the best explanation of moral experience.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it accounts for reasons and moralized conduct without objective value, defends an explanatory standard for evidence, and shows that moral facts neither ground categorical reasons nor contribute indispensable explanatory work.

motionBridge.description: Connect the denial of attitude-independent value with the claim that moral belief lacks the evidence required for moral knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Ground normative reasons in desires, goals, values, or an agent's deliberative perspective rather than categorical demands.
Require justified belief to arise from causally informed explanatory support and show that moral facts are evidentially idle.
Explain the acquisition of concepts and causal models without presupposing contentful appearances accepted as initially true.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for moral judgment and continued moralized conduct through projected values, emotions, and stable concerns.
Interpret mathematical and modal reflection through conceptual application, experiential relations, or a broadened account of analyticity.

sections.title: Objective Value and the Error-Theoretic Burden
sections.rationale: This issue frames the motion-level dispute over whether elementary moral judgments track attitude-independent facts or whether value is exhausted by human attitudes and practices.

sections.title: Desires, Reasons, and Rational Authority
sections.rationale: The existence of categorical reasons is the principal metaphysical pathway between theories of agency and the existence or nonexistence of objective moral obligations.

sections.title: Appearances, Explanation, and Epistemic Foundations
sections.rationale: This issue directly determines whether moral appearances may justify belief prima facie or whether evidence requires causal and best-explanation support that leaves moral facts idle.

sections.title: Moral Belief, Emotion, and Projection
sections.rationale: The causal relationship among judgment, desire, emotion, and conduct bears on whether moral thought responds to facts or projects antecedent evaluative attitudes.

sections.title: A Priori Knowledge, Concepts, and Analyticity
sections.rationale: The scope of a priori justification tests whether reflection can disclose substantive truths about suffering and badness or only relations internal to concepts and their application.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: Objective moral facts do not exist because valuing reflects human attitudes and practices rather than attitude-independent standards ratified by the universe.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the opening statement to Matt, who identifies himself and states the error-theory position in the first person.

response.rationale: This constructive opening states the error-theoretic position and supplies the attitude-and-practice account on which the subsequent con route relies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes a central position, though the supporting inference remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but the relation between social practices, valuing, and the absence of objective standards is not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical denial of objective value exceeds the excerpt's support, which principally describes the social embedding of the speaker's valuing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The social-practice premise is compatible with objective standards, so the decisive inference from practice to nonexistence remains underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited features of valuing are relevant but do not independently establish that attitude-independent standards are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the con motion bridge by expressly denying attitude-independent moral facts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances its own error-theoretic account without materially interpreting a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked excerpt links moral valuing to praise-and-blame practices and asserts that the universe supplies no standards of correctness.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: Moral obligations would require desire-independent categorical reasons, but intelligible reasons arise from promoting desires, so such moral obligations do not exist.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt presents this as his basic reason for rejecting moral facts during his uninterrupted opening statement, repeatedly using first-person formulations.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the principal desire-based account of reasons and connects it to the denial of categorical moral obligations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the central metaphysical route and its intended consequence for morality.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is recoverable, though desires are construed broadly enough to include values and goals, leaving their exact explanatory role somewhat open.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal claim that all intelligible reasons depend on desires is asserted more strongly than the excerpt's supporting analysis warrants.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional path to error theory is intelligible, but the crucial universal premise about reasons remains a material unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move defines categorical normativity clearly but offers limited independent support for reducing all reasons to desire promotion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It closely supports the indispensable con bridge grounding normative reasons in an agent's desires or standpoint.

representationalCharity.rationale: This opening construction does not yet engage a sufficiently developed opposing interpretation to trigger a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source defines categorical reasons as desire-independent and treats morality as requiring them, while advancing desire dependence as exhaustive.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: Evidence supports belief when the belief's truth best explains experience, but moral truths do not best explain moral experience and therefore cannot ground moral knowledge.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Matt's opening statement and expressly identifies his explanationist epistemology and its application to moral intuitions.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes explanationism as the con epistemic standard and applies it directly to the possibility of moral knowledge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives a clear general principle, an application, and the intended skeptical consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear, but the claim that this is generally how evidence and knowledge work ranges beyond the examples without scope restrictions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Treating best explanation as a necessary condition for evidence generally is stronger than the coffee-cup illustration and moral application establish.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference works if explanationism is accepted, but the exclusivity of that epistemic standard is the principal unargued bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The perceptual example illustrates explanatory support but does not establish that every justified belief must meet the proposed standard.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the con route's indispensable explanationist standard and applies it to moral knowledge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive span presents explanationism without yet assessing a developed foundationalist alternative in detail.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked evidence generalizes from perceptual belief to a best-explanation condition for evidence and then applies that condition to morality.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Error theory is less initially plausible than elementary moral judgments that suffering is bad and torturing people for fun is wrong.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly hands the opening statement to Mike, and the new speaker directly discusses Matt's argument and identifies error theory as Matt's view.

components.text: Whether the denial of objective moral facts is better supported than elementary contrary moral judgments.
Whether the premise that reasons cannot exist independently of desires is initially credible.

response.rationale: The move directly compares the initial plausibility of error theory and its desire-based premise with elementary judgments about suffering and torture.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive claims but chiefly shifts comparative plausibility rather than fully answering their supporting arguments.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly comparative and limited to initial plausibility, with concrete elementary judgments identifying the comparison class.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker asserts a comparative plausibility judgment rather than claiming a deductive refutation, matching the intuitive evidence offered.

charity.alternative: Error theory may explain why elementary moral judgments feel compelling while nevertheless treating all of them as false.
charity.decisiveQualification: Initial plausibility alone does not resolve the error theorist's explanatory case.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative-evidence inference is coherent, with the bounded implicit bridge that initial plausibility has defeasible epistemic weight.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete elementary judgments support the comparison, though no fuller account is given for their reliability or independence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the con motion-level denial by placing basic realist judgments against error theory.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies genuine anti-realist premises and compares them fairly, though it does not fully address their explanatory support.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names suffering and torture judgments, compares their plausibility with anti-realist premises, and specifically challenges desire dependence.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Appearances confer defeasible prima facie justification, because denying all appearance-based justification would leave the denial itself unjustified.
moves.attributionBasis: This is part of Huemer's uninterrupted opening statement and is explicitly framed as his own view and his favored argument for it.

components.text: Whether justification must always be earned through best-explanation support rather than appearances.

response.rationale: The move diagnoses the exclusive explanationist demand as self-defeating because the view itself ultimately rests on how things seem to its proponent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the decisive exclusivity premise and states the defeating consequence that the view would itself be unjustified.

precisionFindings.rationale: The appearance principle is expressly limited to prima facie justification in the absence of defeaters, keeping its scope and status clear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The self-defeat argument is carefully conditional, although the claim that all opposing beliefs depend on appearances retains a compressed premise.

charity.alternative: Explanationism may treat the relevant background beliefs as parts of a coherent causal model rather than as accepted appearances.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such a model still needs an account of how its initial experiential and background inputs gain justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-defeat structure is explicit and consistent, with one bounded bridge concerning the unavoidable basis of explanationist beliefs.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument supplies a reasoned internal critique, though it does not independently establish every belief's dependence on propositional appearances.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable pro appearance principle while attacking the con explanationist exclusivity claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply reaches the strongest explanatory alternative and identifies the remaining foundational demand, with only limited development of coherentist options.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source expressly conditions justification on an absence of defeaters and argues that denying appearance-based support undermines the denial itself.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Desires alone cannot explain rational action because deciding which present, future, or imagined desires to follow requires evaluative assessment.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer explicitly labels the target as Matt's argument about reasons and develops counterexamples throughout the remainder of this continuous passage.

components.text: Whether desires alone can explain which actions and desires agents rationally ought to favor.

response.rationale: The reply supplies cases involving present, future, and imagined desires and argues that their rational ordering requires an evaluative judgment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive reduction of reasons to desires and offers counterexamples aimed at its explanatory sufficiency.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between desire and evaluative judgment is clear, though the independence and truth conditions of evaluation remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The counterexample-based conclusion is forceful but appropriately presented as showing explanatory insufficiency rather than a complete metaphysical proof.

charity.alternative: A sophisticated desire theory can rank desires by informed, future, higher-order, or counterfactual preferences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Selecting which ranking rule is rational appears to require a standard not supplied merely by the existence of those desires.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexamples coherently expose the need for a selection standard, leaving only the bounded bridge from evaluation to objective value.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple contrasting cases provide relevant conceptual support, though the move does not fully exclude every sophisticated desire-based standard.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con bridge that grounds all normative reasons in desires or an agent's standpoint.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move considers several expanded desire bases and presses the same explanatory question against them without reducing the view to momentary impulse.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span culminates in the claim that identical desire constraints can accompany rational or irrational conduct, distinguished by evaluation.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: If moral facts entail desire-independent reasons and all reasons depend on desires, then there are no moral facts; evaluating the disputed premise requires comparing the rival worldviews.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Matt to recapitulate the Humean argument, after which Matt restates it and explicitly addresses Mike's objections by name.

components.text: Whether basic moral plausibility defeats the Humean argument for error theory.
Whether cases requiring evaluative assessment refute the premise that all reasons depend on desires.

response.rationale: The reply explicitly restates the Humean syllogism and explains that the disputed desire-dependence premise must be assessed within rival theoretical pictures.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both challenges and clarifies the inference, but largely postpones rather than resolves the dispute over its crucial premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism and its contested premise are recoverable, and the appeal to worldview comparison is identified as the method of assessment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion follows conditionally, but the categorical conclusion remains only as warranted as the expressly disputed universal premise.

charity.alternative: Elementary moral judgments and evaluative counterexamples may provide direct evidence against universal desire dependence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Restating the valid conditional inference does not independently establish the universal desire-dependence premise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The formal inference is clear and valid, with the material limitation that its decisive universal premise remains defended mainly by framework comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The restatement precisely identifies the premise requiring support but adds limited evidence establishing that premise over the rival account.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the con motion bridge by explicitly connecting desire dependence to the nonexistence of moral facts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the opposing objections and locates the real disagreement, though it gives their direct evidential force limited treatment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states the two-premise Humean argument and identifies broad desires, including values and goals, as the alleged basis of all reasons.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: Overpowering desires do not refute a desire-based theory because normative weight tracks a desire's centrality to the agent's self-conception rather than its momentary motivational force.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly introduces Huemer's partying-student objection and answers it continuously through the discussion of Odysseus completed in the locked lookahead.

components.text: Whether cases of overpowering or conflicting desire show that desire-based reasons cannot distinguish rational action.

response.rationale: The reply rejects proportionalism and offers centrality to self-conception as a desire-based ranking principle for the counterexamples.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the strongest motivational-force counterexample with a distinct account of normative weight.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternative is clear, but centrality to self-conception is not given sufficiently precise criteria to determine rankings independently.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The proposal is framed as an account rather than a demonstration, but its claimed normative authority remains somewhat stronger than its support.

charity.alternative: The counterexamples challenge desire theories generally because any ranking of desires may require an independent evaluative standard.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting proportionalism avoids motivational strength but does not yet explain why self-conception has normative authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response blocks one inference from strong motivation to strong reason, but leaves a material bridge from self-centrality to normative weight.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The proposed hierarchy explains relevant cases plausibly, though independent support for privileging self-conception is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central desire-based-reasons bridge by supplying a ranking mechanism within the agent's standpoint.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately distinguishes motivational force from normative weight, though it does not fully meet the deeper authority objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source expressly rejects proportionalism and proposes centrality to an agent's conception of self as the alternative determinant of weight.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Centrality to self-conception does not by itself confer rational authority, since weakness of will and arbitrary higher-order desires can occur without a principled hierarchy.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn develops several first-person objections to the immediately preceding account of desire centrality.

components.text: Whether centrality or higher-order status itself gives a desire greater normative authority.
Whether a desire-only hierarchy can supply a nonarbitrary standard of rational ranking.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the proposed hierarchy's missing authority principle and uses arbitrary higher-order urges to show that formal rank is insufficient.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the missing inference, tests it with a targeted counterexample, and states why the desire hierarchy does not solve it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is narrowly directed at authority by centrality or order, and the arbitrary-urge case clearly specifies the counterexample.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims insufficiency rather than proving every hierarchy impossible, which fits the counterexample and explicit questions it raises.

charity.alternative: Self-conception may reflect stable, reflectively endorsed commitments rather than any spontaneous higher-order desire.
charity.decisiveQualification: Stability and endorsement still require an account of why they confer rational rather than merely motivational authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample directly separates higher-order status from authority and exposes the missing premise without relying on equivocation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The arbitrary higher-order desire is a specific and probative conceptual test, though it does not exclude every substantive self-conception theory.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con desire-based-reasons bridge by challenging its proposed source of rational authority.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection reaches a sophisticated hierarchical interpretation and preserves its relevant distinction while pressing the unresolved normative bridge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked evidence asks why second-order desires are authoritative and presents a baseless spontaneous desire to alter desires as a counterexample.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Abandoning belief in objective moral facts would substantially alter many people's desires, emotions, charitable conduct, and interpretation of ordinary actions.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers the opposing hypothetical in the first person and generalizes the behavioral consequences to many people.

components.text: Whether stable concerns and self-conception fully account for moralized motivation without objective moral belief.

response.rationale: The reply argues that removing objective moral belief would alter desires, conduct, and interpretation, challenging the sufficiency of antecedent concerns.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the motivational implication but relies substantially on predicted reactions rather than directly analyzing the self-conception mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The personal prediction is clear, but its generalization to many people and the extent of substantial change are only loosely bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The first-person counterfactual is credible as testimony, while broader behavioral generalizations receive limited independent support.

charity.alternative: An error theorist can retain charitable desires and moralized concepts after abandoning belief in objective moral facts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Some conduct may persist even if the interpretation, emotional force, or pattern of motivation changes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterfactual coherently bears on causal efficacy, with an implicit bridge from predicted change to the broader role of moral belief.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Personal testimony and conceptual examples are relevant but weak support for the asserted effects across many people's conduct.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the con subsidiary projection-and-motivation account, though it does not reach a central route requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows that ordinary attitudes matter and focuses on changed motivational effects, though the prediction remains largely introspective.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source predicts radical changes in interpretation and behavior if moral belief were excised and illustrates this with ordinary moralized concepts.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: Moral belief projects antecedent values onto the world, so abandoning belief in objective morality would ordinarily leave the underlying attitudes and conduct intact.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly answers the predicted behavioral change and presents the standard error-theoretic projective explanation in his own voice.

components.text: Whether abandoning objective moral belief would ordinarily eliminate or substantially alter underlying values and conduct.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the behavioral counterfactual by distinguishing projected objective belief from the antecedent values that generate it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the predicted motivational change and supplies an alternative causal account of belief and conduct.

precisionFindings.rationale: Projection and antecedent values are used consistently, but the claim that conduct would ordinarily remain intact has an imprecise population scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The projective account is presented as a probable causal explanation, but stability of conduct is not independently demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Objective moral belief may itself reshape desires, emotions, interpretation, and action rather than merely express prior values.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing antecedent values can produce moral belief does not establish that the resulting belief has no reciprocal causal effects.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The projection model is internally coherent, with a materially compressed inference from causal origin to continued motivational independence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Humean projection description is a relevant mechanism but is asserted without comparative evidence against reciprocal-causation alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the con subsidiary bridge accounting for moral belief and conduct through projected antecedent values.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the claimed behavioral effects but underdevelops the strongest feedback interpretation of moral belief's causal role.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes the mind as spreading desires onto the world and treating the resulting appearance of external endorsement as moral belief.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Intellectual moral judgments can override stronger emotional attractions, while beliefs about justice can shape the emotions that motivate intervention.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker announces two points and supports both with personal and interpersonal examples directed against the prior account.

components.text: Whether moral judgment merely projects antecedent emotions and therefore lacks independent effects on conduct.
Whether stable passions or self-conception can exhaustively explain apparently intellectual choice.

response.rationale: The reply offers cases where intellectual judgment overrides emotional attraction and where justice judgments shape the emotions supporting intervention.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly targets the claimed causal ordering with two counterexamples addressing both action and emotion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The modal claim that judgments can direct conduct is narrower than a universal causal thesis, and the two mechanisms are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples are used to establish possible counterinstances to a one-way projection story, a force well matched to their support.

charity.alternative: Apparently intellectual judgments may express stable, less phenomenally salient cold passions rather than independent cognition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Labeling the stable concern a passion does not by itself explain judgment's apparent selection among competing emotional attractions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples coherently undermine an exhaustive antecedent-emotion account, with only a bounded bridge from introspection to causal direction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific personal and interpersonal examples support counterpossibility, though they do not establish the general frequency of judgment-led motivation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the con subsidiary projection-and-motivation bridge through direct counterexamples to its causal account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents cases suited to the sophisticated cold-passion interpretation while preserving the unresolved causal-order question.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source contrasts cost-effectiveness judgment with emotional appeal and describes beliefs about injustice as influencing emotions and intervention.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: Emotions generally cause moral judgments, while apparently unemotional deliberation can still express stable cold passions connected to an agent's self-conception.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly invokes an empirical model, his own experience, and a Humean distinction to answer the preceding examples.

components.text: Whether apparently intellectual moral judgments can motivate action independently of antecedent passions.

response.rationale: The reply answers the examples by invoking an emotion-first empirical model and classifying low-affect stable commitments as cold passions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the examples with a relevant reinterpretation, though it does not fully adjudicate their causal ordering.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hot-versus-cold distinction is intelligible, but expanding passion to cover apparently unemotional commitments risks explanatory looseness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The general tendency claim is moderately framed, but the locked excerpt offers limited empirical detail supporting the causal generalization.

charity.alternative: Judgment can select conduct against stronger emotional attraction and later generate an emotion aligned with the judgment.
charity.decisiveQualification: A cold-passion label must independently identify an antecedent cause rather than redescribe any motivating judgment after the fact.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reinterpretation is compatible with the examples, but compatibility alone does not establish the claimed causal priority of passion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The empirical model and personal report are relevant, though the excerpt provides little comparative evidence against judgment-first causation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the con subsidiary projection-and-motivation bridge by defending emotion-first causal ordering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply engages the strongest cases but does not fully meet the concern that its broadened passion category may become unfalsifiable.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes conduct-related emotion and Hume's hot-and-cold passion distinction to reinterpret allegedly unemotional judgments.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: Experience supports belief through background causal understanding, not because experience possesses propositional content that directly confers prima facie justification.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly addresses Matt, and the ensuing first-person account explicitly contrasts Mike's propositional-content view with a causal explanation.

components.text: Whether experiential propositional content itself confers prima facie justification.

response.rationale: The reply directly denies content-based justification and replaces it with background causal beliefs connecting experiences to their worldly causes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive epistemic mechanism and supplies a concrete alternative account using perceptual belief.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal alternative and rejected propositional-content account are clearly separated, though the source of background justification remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The perceptual causal story is plausible, but the stronger exclusion of content-based prima facie support is not fully established.

charity.alternative: Appearances can provide defeasible initial justification while causal background knowledge increases or defeats that support.
charity.decisiveQualification: The existence of causal mediation does not by itself show that appearance content contributes no initial justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternative causal account is coherent, with a bounded but important missing account of how the background causal beliefs gain justification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The coffee-cup mechanism is specific and relevant, though it does not discriminate conclusively between causal and hybrid appearance accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con explanationist-evidence bridge and attacks the pro appearance principle's proposed mechanism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately distinguishes the rival mechanism but treats the causal story too readily as exclusive rather than potentially complementary.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked excerpt says perceptual justification arises from background causal belief about coffee-cup experiences, not propositional experiential content.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Causal and best-explanation reasoning cannot begin unless agents initially accept that things are generally as they appear to be.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers Lutz's causal account, defines experiential content, and develops Huemer's foundational regress objection to explanationism.

components.text: Whether background causal and best-explanation reasoning can justify beliefs without prior acceptance of appearances.
Whether best-explanation support can serve as the exclusive foundation of justification.

response.rationale: The reply identifies a regress in appealing to background causal beliefs and argues that explanation assessment must begin from accepted appearances.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly targets the alternative mechanism, diagnoses its foundational dependence, and states the defeating regress consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is confined to epistemic priority and general initial acceptance, not the indefeasibility or universal truth of appearances.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessary-priority claim is supported by the stated regress challenge and is qualified as general initial acceptance rather than certainty.

charity.alternative: A coherent causal web might mutually support experiences and background beliefs without a privileged foundational appearance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mutual coherence still requires some epistemic access to the data and apparent relations by which explanatory fit is assessed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress objection is explicit, consistent, and directly exposes the presupposition involved in judging one explanation better than another.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The internal epistemic argument is well developed, with only a bounded gap concerning possible nonfoundational mutual-support accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con central explanationist bridge and supports the epistemic priority component of the pro appearance principle.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply directly anticipates appeal to additional background beliefs and traces their provenance, though it does not exhaust every coherentist formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence asks how best explanation is known, traces background beliefs backward, and concludes that agents initially accept how things seem.

moves.speaker: Matt Lutz
moves.proposition: Mathematical reflection supplies experiential evidence about correct conceptual application and relations rather than justification through intellectual seemings whose content is a mathematical proposition.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator's mathematical challenge is directed to Matt, and the answer expressly ties his earlier explanationist account to conceptual structure.

components.text: Whether intellectual seemings with propositional content are required to explain a priori mathematical justification.

response.rationale: The reply accepts mathematical reflection as evidence but analyzes it through felt confidence and correct conceptual relations rather than propositional seemings.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the broader appearance account through a relevant mathematical case, though it only partly addresses epistemic priority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternative is recoverable, but the relation among sensation, confidence, conceptual application, and evidential force remains partly unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker explicitly allows mathematical reflection to count as evidence and cautiously disputes only the propositional-seeming interpretation.

charity.alternative: The feeling that a mathematical proposition seems true may itself be an intellectual appearance with that proposition as content.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reclassifying the phenomenology as confidence or sensation does not yet explain why the specific proposition is justified.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conceptual alternative is possible and consistent, but the bridge from felt confidence to justified correct application remains materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The introspective mathematical example is specific, yet it offers limited support for preferring the conceptual account over propositional appearance.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports the con subsidiary empiricist account of a priori reflection rather than a central motion bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the phenomenon and evidential role, but its competing account leaves the content-specific warrant materially compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts mathematical reflection as evidence, describes repeating a mathematical thought, and attributes its force to sensation and confidence.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Necessary a priori truths such as the incompatibility of being wholly red and wholly blue appear synthetic because synonym substitution does not reduce them to logical truths.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn follows Lutz's self-identification as an empiricist and presents Huemer's familiar synthetic-a-priori counterexamples as a direct challenge.

components.text: Whether substantive necessary knowledge can be reduced to conceptual application or analyticity.

response.rationale: The reply offers color incompatibility as a necessary a priori truth and tests whether synonym substitution can reduce it to a logical truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly challenges the empiricist conceptual account with a standard but specifically developed counterexample.

precisionFindings.rationale: The example, modal status, and proposed test for analyticity are all clear, while the conclusion is appropriately framed as appearance.
